title: Strong Passwords
about: How passwords get guessed, and how to make yours hard to crack.

cards.prompt: **Drag the slider** until a computer would need **100+ years** to guess this password.
cards.explanation: A computer makes about a **billion guesses a second**, and each extra letter multiplies its work by **26**. **Length** is what makes a password strong.
cards.hint: Drag the slider to the right and watch the time shoot up.
cards.nudge: Keep going: every extra letter multiplies the time by 26.

cards.prompt: Which password would take a computer **longer** to guess?

options.nudge: Symbols help a little, but it's only 8 characters. Think back to the slider.
A word plus a year is one of the first things guessed, and it's fairly short.

cards.hint: What made the time shoot up on the slider?
cards.explanation: **Length wins.** Four random words make a long password that's easy to remember: a **passphrase**. Short ones with symbols are guessed far sooner.

cards.title: Length wins
cards.body:
Capitals, numbers and symbols help a little. **Length** helps a lot more.

Best: a **passphrase** of **four or more random words**, at least **15 characters**, like `violet cactus harbour pepper`. Australia's cyber security experts at cyber.gov.au recommend it.

Guessers try common passwords (`password123`, `qwerty`), names, birthdays, song lyrics and swaps like `@` for `a` first.

cards.prompt: Is each password **easy to guess** or **hard to guess**?

items.label: Your pet's name and birth year
A long random mix of 16 characters

cards.explanation: Common passwords, patterns, names and swaps are **tried first**. Random words, or a long random mix, must be found by trying every combination.
cards.hint: Would a guesser try it early: a common password, a pattern, a name or a swap?
cards.nudge: Look at each one again: is it on a guesser's early list, or long and random?

cards.prompt: Now the limit is **10 characters**. Reach **100 years** by choosing which kinds of characters to use.
cards.explanation: More kinds of characters means more to try, so a **short random** password can reach 100 years. But it's hard to remember, so long passphrases suit people better.
cards.hint: Set the length to 10, then turn on more kinds of characters.
cards.nudge: Push the length to 10, then add kinds of characters until it passes 100 years.

cards.prompt: Which of these makes the **best** passphrase?

options.nudge: Song lyrics are in guessing lists. The words need to be random, not ones that belong together.
Pet names and birth years are easy for someone to find out or guess.
Symbol swaps are one of the first tricks a guesser tries, and it's short.

cards.explanation: Four **random, unrelated** words are long, easy to remember and hard to guess. Lyrics, personal details and swaps are all tried early.
cards.hint: Look for words that have nothing to do with each other, or with you.

cards.prompt: Your friend Mia's new passphrase is a line from her favourite song: five words, 26 characters.

choices.text: Not really: song lines are in guessing lists
choices.consequence: Right. Guessers try lyrics and famous lines early. Length only helps when the words are random.

choices.text: Yes: it's over 15 characters, so it's long enough
choices.consequence: Length isn't enough on its own. A famous line is in guessing lists, so it falls early.

choices.text: Yes, if she adds a symbol like ! to the end
choices.consequence: A symbol on the end is one of the first tricks guessers try. The words need to be random.

steps.text: Mia asks what she should do instead.

choices.text: Pick four or more random words that don't belong together
choices.consequence: Now it's long **and** unpredictable. She can still picture the words to remember them.

choices.text: Pick a line from an old song hardly anyone knows
choices.consequence: Guessing lists hold huge numbers of songs, not just popular ones. The words need to be random.

cards.explanation: A passphrase needs **random** words. Lyrics and quotes are long but predictable, so guessers try them early.
cards.hint: Length is one thing that makes a passphrase strong. What's the other?

cards.prompt: A game website emails you: it had a [[data breach]], and passwords were stolen.

steps.text: Attackers try stolen passwords on other sites, and you used this one for your **email** too. What do you do first?

choices.text: Change your email password to a new, unique one
choices.consequence: Good. Your email is the most important account: it can reset all the others.

choices.text: Nothing. It's only a game account
choices.consequence: The same password opens your email too. Attackers try stolen passwords on other sites.
The stolen password still opens your email. That's the one to change first.

steps.text: Your email is safe again. What about the game account?

choices.text: Give it its own new password too
choices.consequence: Now each account has its own password, so one leak can't open the other.

choices.text: Use your new email password for the game as well
choices.consequence: Then the next breach could open your email again. Every account needs its own password.

cards.explanation: Change a stolen password everywhere you used it, starting with your **email**, which can reset the rest. Every account needs its own password.
cards.hint: Which account could be used to reset all your others?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- Guessers try **common passwords**, names and patterns first.
- **Length** wins: a **passphrase** is four or more **random** words.
- Give every account its **own** password.

Next: a second lock on the door.
